drivingQuestion: Does 'upon the wood' permit placement adjacent to the wood?

segments.he: בָּעֵי רַבִּי יִצְחָק נַפָּחָא: אֵבָרִין שֶׁסִּידְּרָן בְּצִידֵּי הַמַּעֲרָכָה, מַהוּ? אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר ״עַל״ מַמָּשׁ – לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ,
segments.en: «Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa raises a dilemma:» With regard to the «limbs» of an offering «that» a priest «arranged adjacent to the arrangement» of wood on the altar, «what is» the halakha? The Gemara explains: «Do not raise the dilemma according to» the opinion «of the one who says» that the phrase «“upon [al]» the wood” is meant «literally,»
«as “upon [al]» the wood” «is written,» and not: Next to the wood.

segments.he: כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ, אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר ״עַל״ בְּסָמוּךְ, מַאי? הָכָא נָמֵי ״עַל״ בְּסָמוּךְ, אוֹ דִלְמָא ״עַל הָעֵצִים״ דּוּמְיָא דְּ״עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״ – מָה הָתָם עַל מַמָּשׁ, אַף הָכָא נָמֵי עַל מַמָּשׁ? תֵּיקוּ.
segments.en: «When should you raise the dilemma?» Raise it «according to» the opinion «of the one who says» in the mishna (96a) that the term «“upon [al]”» (see Numbers 2:20) means «adjacent to.» According to that tanna, «what» is the halakha in this case? Is it explained that «here, too,» the phrase «“upon [al]» the wood” can mean «adjacent to» the wood? «Or perhaps,» the phrase “upon [al] the wood that is on the fire upon the altar” teaches that «“upon the wood”» is to be understood as «similar to “upon the altar”: Just as there “upon» the altar” is meant «literally, so too here,» the phrase «“upon» the wood” is meant «literally.» The Gemara comments: No answer was found, and the dilemma «shall stand» unresolved.
